mainEntity.name: Why use the lowest common denominator instead of just multiplying the denominators?

acceptedAnswer.text: Any common denominator works, but the lowest one keeps the numbers small and often skips a later simplification step. For 5/6 + 1/4, multiplying gives 26/24 which must be reduced to 13/12; the LCD 12 gives 13/12 directly.

mainEntity.name: How can I tell whether a decimal will terminate or repeat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Reduce the fraction, then factor the denominator. If it contains only 2s and 5s, the decimal terminates (3/8 = 0.375). Any other prime factor makes it repeat (1/3 = 0.(3), 1/7 = 0.(142857)).
Only the fraction as a whole carries a sign: −3/4 = 3/(−4) = −(3/4). This calculator keeps the denominator positive and puts the sign on the numerator (or in front of a mixed number).

mainEntity.name: How do I convert a mixed number to an improper fraction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator: 2 1/3 = (2 × 3 + 1)/3 = 7/3. Going the other way, divide and keep the remainder: 7/3 = 2 remainder 1, so 2 1/3.

mainEntity.name: Why can’t the denominator be zero?

acceptedAnswer.text: Division by zero is undefined. A denominator of 0 would mean splitting something into zero parts. Dividing by a fraction whose numerator is 0 is likewise undefined.

It writes a number as a whole part plus 1 over another whole part plus 1 over …: 17/12 = 1 + 1/(2 + 1/(2 + 1/2)), written [1; 2, 2, 2]. The quotients are exactly the ones produced by Euclid’s algorithm.
